chapter_theme: Empty speech, especially before many, ruins the speaker's standing and even his claim to being fully human. The chapter ranks uselessness of speech as a graver failing than unkindness or lack of grace, and ends with a bare rule.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the fault of useless speech (191-196), the merit of refraining from it (197-199), and the rule of what to say and not say (200).

191.reading: A person who talks emptily to the irritation of many ends up despised by all.
191.nuance: The verse says only 'many'. Parimelazhagar narrows them to the discerning, which turns the move from 'many' to 'all' into a causal chain: once the wise are repelled, everyone else follows.

192.reading: Saying useless things before many is worse than doing what is unwelcome to one's friends.
192.nuance: The ranking is startling: a word to an audience outweighs a deed against a friend. Parimelazhagar's explanation is that the talk brings more disgrace, so his measure is the speaker's standing and not the harm done.

193.reading: Expansive talk about useless things itself declares that the speaker is one without நயன்.
193.nuance: No one needs to accuse the talker, because the speech testifies against him. நயன் shifts through this chapter: Parimelazhagar takes it as liking in 192 and as justice here, so the word should not be given a single translation.

194.reading: Graceless words that serve no purpose, spoken among many, lack நயன் and take a person away from what is good.

positions.position: The words fall short of justice toward the listeners, and cost the speaker his good qualities.
positions.quote: அவை அவர்மாட்டு நீதியோடு படாவாய், அவனை நற்குணங்களின் நீக்கும்.

positions.position: நயன் is even-handedness, and it is the speaker who loses that balance and falls from goodness.
நயன் is the gladness of the gathering, and such words destroy it along with good.

195.reading: If those of gentle nature speak useless things, their worth departs and the regard it earned goes with it.
195.nuance: The verse aims at the good, not the habitual babbler of 196. Standing already earned is not secure against this one lapse.

196.reading: Don't call a person who keeps up useless talk a man; call him chaff among people.
196.nuance: For Parimelazhagar the image means a husk without the kernel of understanding, so the talk reveals emptiness and doesn't merely offend.

positions.position: பாராட்டுவான் is one who says such things repeatedly: the fault is the habit.
He is one who prizes and celebrates useless speech: the fault is the relish.
He is one who hopes to profit from empty talk: the fault is the motive.

197.reading: Let the worthy say what lacks நயன் if they must; it is good that they not say what lacks use.
197.nuance: The concession is rhetorical, as Parimelazhagar observes: 'even if they say it' implies they should not. Its force is the comparison, which keeps the sting whichever sense of நயன் is taken.

positions.position: நயன் is justice, so even speech at odds with justice is ranked less bad than useless speech.
positions.quote: நயன் இலவற்றினும் பயன் இல தீய என்பதாம்.

positions.position: நயன் is pleasantness, so the worthy may say what is unsweet, which is a much milder claim.

198.reading: Those whose understanding searches out rare ends do not say what lacks great use.
198.nuance: The bar rises here from useless to not greatly useful, and Parimelazhagar draws this out: words of small use are excluded too. His identification of the rare ends with release and higher destinies is his own; Manakkudavar says only 'rare matters'.

positions.position: The rare ends are release and passage to higher worlds.
positions.quote: அறிதற்கு அரிய பயன்களாவன: வீடு பேறும் மேற்கதிச் செலவும் முதலாயின.

199.reading: Those of stainless sight, freed from delusion, do not say meaningless things even by a lapse.
199.nuance: பொச்சாந்தும் moves the claim from choice to nature: for such people the restraint survives inattention.

200.reading: Say what among words has use; do not say what among words has none.
200.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes that சொல்லில் is grammatically surplus and kept for the figure of repeated words. It may be a quiet wit that a chapter against waste in speech ends on a deliberate surplus, though that is my reading and no commentator's.

positions.position: சொல்லில் means 'among words': the verse sorts words into two kinds.
The first சொல்லில் means 'if you speak', which leaves silence as an option.

links.note: 100 calls harsh speech a raw fruit taken over a ripe one, yet on Kalaignar's reading 197 tolerates unsweet speech before useless speech. Sweetness is not the highest test of a word.
291 defines truthfulness as speech without harm; 200 demands use. Harmless idle talk passes the one test and fails the other, so the two chapters set different standards for speech.
645 echoes the same imperative and raises the standard: useful is not enough if some other word could defeat it.
Both deny full humanity by appearance alone: chaff has the look of grain, and the base look like people. For the Kural, being human is something a person can fail at.
Both use 'even by forgetting', 199 for the speech of the clear-sighted and 204 for plotting harm. The first describes an achieved nature, and the second commands what such a nature would be.

source_issues: 191: Manakkudavar's text begins mid-verse with a corrupted fragment (னேல்லாரு மெள்ளப் படும்), but its gloss is usable.
196: the verse text reads பராட்டு வானை, with a short first vowel, while Parimelazhagar reads பாராட்டுவான்.
